pages.intent: why the format question is urgent: the market is moving away from the large-store model
pages.message: Grocery spend grows £12.9bn by 2028, yet large stores' share falls from 47% to 36% as shoppers trade the weekly shop for top-ups

exhibits.reader_must_see: that the large-store channel loses more share than any other channel gains, while discounters and online climb
exhibits.comparison: each channel's share of regional grocery spend in 2019, 2025 and 2028 against its own earlier share
exhibits.data: five channels by three points in time, shares of spend that sum to 100 at each point

forms_considered.form: slope lines of channel share
forms_considered.reason: chosen: each channel's change is its own slope, and the steepest fall is the large-store line

forms_considered.form: 100% stacked columns by year
forms_considered.reason: only the bottom segment shares a baseline, so the middle channels' changes cannot be compared

forms_considered.form: table of shares by year
forms_considered.reason: carries every figure but makes the reader subtract to find the direction

exhibits.why: the claim is a direction and a size of change per channel, which slopes on one scale show without arithmetic
exhibits.marks: the large-store line in persimmon with its 47% and 36% labelled at the ends; the other four lines grey-blue with their end values and names at the right

exhibits.reader_must_see: that main weekly shop trips fell by more than a quarter while top-up and food-for-now trips rose
exhibits.comparison: trips per household per week in 2025 against 2019, mission by mission
exhibits.data: four shopping missions by two years, a count of trips per household per week

forms_considered.form: paired horizontal bars by mission
forms_considered.reason: chosen: the two years sit side by side for each mission, and long mission names read on the left

forms_considered.form: column chart of the change in trips
forms_considered.reason: shows the change but drops the base, so a fall of 0.4 trips reads the same on any base

forms_considered.form: line chart over years
forms_considered.reason: only two years are measured; a line would invent the path between them

exhibits.why: the reader compares each mission's two bars and reads the main shop's fall against its own base
exhibits.marks: the 2025 main-shop bar in persimmon with its value; a label at its end saying the fall in percent; 2019 bars in grey-blue

pages.intent: the economics of each format, and which ones earn their capital
pages.message: Superstores take 58% of Brindle's capital but return 4.9%, under half the 12% hurdle; neighbourhood stores return 19.5%

exhibits.reader_must_see: each format's full store P&L line by line, so the team can check it against its own numbers, with the superstore return picked out
exhibits.comparison: the four formats against each other and against the whole estate, metric by metric
exhibits.data: four formats and a total by twelve metrics in mixed units: counts, square feet, pounds, percentages

forms_considered.form: format P&L table with formats as columns
forms_considered.reason: chosen: mixed units sit one per row and each row reads across the four formats and the total

forms_considered.form: small multiples of bars per metric
forms_considered.reason: twelve small charts would be unreadable at this size and lose the figures the team checks

exhibits.chosen_form: format P&L table with formats as columns
exhibits.why: a lookup page for an executive team that knows its P&Ls: every figure must be findable, and the row order runs from size to return
exhibits.marks: the superstore cash-return cell in persimmon bold; the return row bold for every format

exhibits.reader_must_see: which formats clear the 12% hurdle and by how far the superstore misses it
exhibits.comparison: each format's cash return on invested capital against the 12% hurdle and the estate's average
exhibits.data: one value per format plus the estate total, percentages from 4.9 to 19.5

forms_considered.form: columns of cash return with a hurdle line
forms_considered.reason: chosen: heights against one baseline and a line at 12% show who clears it

forms_considered.form: dot plot of return by format
forms_considered.reason: five dots carry less weight than the decision deserves and invite a misleading zero-less axis

forms_considered.form: bars of return minus hurdle
forms_considered.reason: a signed gap hides the level the finance director quotes

exhibits.chosen_form: columns of cash return with a hurdle line
exhibits.why: the decision is a threshold: a column under the line fails, and the line is labelled with its value
exhibits.marks: the superstore column in persimmon; a dashed hurdle line labelled Hurdle 12%; the estate column in grey-blue; values on every column

pages.intent: where the growth in demand is and how little of it Brindle holds
pages.message: Brindle's share of wallet is 12.9% where spend is flat and 5.0% where it grows: the three growth segments hold 57% of spend

exhibits.reader_must_see: each segment's size, growth, Brindle's share and what it shops for, as a profile the team can quote
exhibits.comparison: the five segments against each other and against the market total
exhibits.data: five segments by eight fields: households, spend, growth, share of wallet, Brindle sales, mission and format, with a total

forms_considered.form: segment profile table with a totals row
forms_considered.reason: chosen: figures and words for each segment read across one row and the figures tie to the market

forms_considered.form: five segment cards
forms_considered.reason: cards separate the figures so they cannot be compared down a column

exhibits.chosen_form: segment profile table with a totals row
exhibits.why: it is the reference the team will come back to; columns let the reader compare shares and growth down the page
exhibits.marks: the share-of-wallet cells of the three growth segments in persimmon bold

exhibits.reader_must_see: that the segments right of the market growth line sit under Brindle's average share, and the slow ones above it
exhibits.comparison: each segment's spend growth against Brindle's share of its wallet, both against the market's own growth and Brindle's average
exhibits.data: five points, growth from -0.6% to 7.9% a year against share of wallet from 3.3% to 13.3%

forms_considered.form: scatter of growth against share of wallet with two reference lines
forms_considered.reason: chosen: the two thresholds divide the plane and the growth segments fall in the low-share quadrant

forms_considered.form: paired bars of growth and share
forms_considered.reason: two scales side by side make the reader join them by eye

forms_considered.form: bubble chart sized by spend
forms_considered.reason: would show size too, but cannot carry the reference lines that make the argument; spend is written in each label instead

exhibits.chosen_form: scatter of growth against share of wallet with two reference lines
exhibits.why: the claim is a negative relation between where spend grows and where Brindle is strong, which two lines on a scatter state plainly
exhibits.marks: growth segments in persimmon and core segments in navy, each point labelled with its name and spend; a dashed line at Brindle's 8.4% average and one at the market's 3.5% growth, each labelled

pages.intent: what to do with each of the 214 stores
pages.message: 128 of 214 stores miss the 12% hurdle: reformat 64 where catchments grow, right-size 49 and exit 15 where they do not

exhibits.reader_must_see: every store placed by its return and its catchment growth, and the four action zones the two thresholds cut
exhibits.comparison: each store's cash return against the 12% hurdle and its catchment growth against 1.5% a year
exhibits.data: 214 stores, each with a cash return from about -6% to 31% and a catchment growth from about -4% to 8%, in five action groups

forms_considered.form: store scatter with hurdle and growth thresholds
forms_considered.reason: chosen: every store is visible and its zone is read from where it falls, so the rule is seen to be applied, not asserted

forms_considered.form: 2x2 matrix of store counts
forms_considered.reason: shows the counts but hides how close many stores sit to a line, which the property director will ask

forms_considered.form: histogram of returns by format
forms_considered.reason: shows the return problem but not the catchment, which decides reformat against right-size

exhibits.chosen_form: store scatter with hurdle and growth thresholds
exhibits.why: the decision is a rule on two measures, and a scatter with the two lines drawn shows both the rule and the stores it sorts
exhibits.marks: stores under the hurdle in persimmon, exits in near-black, the rest grey-blue; labelled hurdle and growth lines; a labelled box round the exit zone; zone names with counts in the four quadrants

exhibits.reader_must_see: what each action covers in stores, sales, EBITDA and capital, and what it costs and earns by 2028
exhibits.comparison: the five actions against each other and against the estate total
exhibits.data: five actions and a total by eight columns: rule, stores, large stores, sales, EBITDA, return, capex and uplift

forms_considered.form: action summary table with a totals row
forms_considered.reason: chosen: the estate ties out in one grid and each action reads across

forms_considered.form: stacked bar of stores by action
forms_considered.reason: carries the counts only, not the money the decision turns on

exhibits.chosen_form: action summary table with a totals row
exhibits.why: the finance director checks that the actions add back to the estate, which a totals row shows
exhibits.marks: the three action rows below the hurdle with their names in persimmon; the totals row bold under a rule

pages.intent: what the programme delivers, when, and for how much capital
pages.message: The plan lifts store EBITDA 42% to £323m by 2028 on £387m of capex; reformats carry 60% of the gain

exhibits.reader_must_see: how each lever moves store EBITDA from £227m to £323m, and that reformats are the largest step
exhibits.comparison: each lever's contribution against the others and against the 2025 starting point
exhibits.data: a starting total, five signed steps and an ending total in pounds millions, four up and one down

forms_considered.form: EBITDA bridge
forms_considered.reason: chosen: steps from a start to an end show each lever's size and sign in sequence

forms_considered.form: stacked column of 2028 EBITDA by source
forms_considered.reason: hides the drag from unchanged stores, which is negative

forms_considered.form: table of levers
forms_considered.reason: carries the figures, which the roadmap table already does, but not the relative size

exhibits.why: a bridge is how a finance director reads a plan: start, levers, end, every step tied
exhibits.marks: the reformat step in persimmon, other gains green and the drag red, totals in navy; each step labelled with its signed value

exhibits.reader_must_see: the phasing of each workstream by year with its stores, capex, uplift and the gate the team must pass
exhibits.comparison: the workstreams against each other, and each year against the next
exhibits.data: five workstreams by three years of store counts, with stores, capex, uplift and a gate in words, and a total

forms_considered.form: roadmap table with years as columns
forms_considered.reason: chosen: counts per year, money and the decision gate sit in one row per workstream and the money ties

forms_considered.form: Gantt bars of workstreams
forms_considered.reason: shows timing but not how many stores each year, nor the money

exhibits.chosen_form: roadmap table with years as columns
exhibits.why: the team must agree the phasing and gates; a table lets them edit a count and see the money beside it
exhibits.marks: the reformat row in persimmon bold; the totals row bold under a rule
